utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you said relevance is unclear. Mr. Traldi explained the relevance. You had an opportunity to respond to that. The Chamber has decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want us to reconsider it, file a motion to that in that respect and explain whether all the requirements for reconsideration are met, and we'll consider such a motion. We move one to the remainder. That is, 2926 and following.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's also Zvornik Brigade, about what Mr. Ewan Brown said that he did -- could not testify because he did not deal with this issue at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It goes to the same issue and is addressed in the same part of P2863, his 92 ter statement. The Defence was certainly aware that he had offered conclusions about a small quantity of Drina Corps documents, not about -- not about events necessarily but about how they related to principles of command and control and dissemination of strategic decisions. And again, I'd refer the Chamber to page 8 and also the top of page 9 of the witness's 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object to admission according to the testimony, live testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask that if Mr. Lukic is going to pursue that argument, that he provide a transcript reference for the testimony he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] standing on my feet, but I -- I'm sure [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your microphone was not activated, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I said that I'm sure that I asked this -- Mr. Brown to testify on some issues in regard of [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. Mr. Lukic, it appears to me that you are prepared but not fully prepared to deal with these matters, because if you are referring to the testimony of Mr. Brown then, of course, it should be clear what portion. The Chamber would like to know that as well in order to avoid that we give decisions which you are then unhappy with. Therefore, I suggest that you prepare in more detail and that we then deal with the matter on from 2926 soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And most likely on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Traldi, I think it's in your hands as well, the admission of the portions of the transcript of the 37th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly in relation to the evidence by Mr. Okun. I think the Chamber asked itself and asked the Prosecution whether we really needed all the 153 pages, and I do understand that you have reduced to them to 26 of the most relevant pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: 26 in the English, Your Honour. I don't know the number of B/C/S pages off the top of my head. About 19, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, this new, I would say, excerpts of the 37th Session uploaded now under number 65 ter 02388a. Any objections against admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02388a receives number P3076, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3076 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then before we continue, the Chamber would like to deliver a decision, which is the decision on the Prosecution's motion for partial reconsideration of the Chamber's decision on the 16th Rule 92 bis motion. In this motion, which was filed on the 28th of October, 2013, in the motion, the Prosecution requests that the Chamber reconsiders its decision of the 4th of October of this year, wherein it provisionally admitted a portion of the tendered evidence of Witness Ljubomir Mitrovic. The Defence did not file a response to the motion. The Chamber recalls and refers to the applicable law governing reconsideration requests as set out in its previous decision of the 29th of June, 2012; and to the applicable law concerning admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis as set out in its decision of the 19th of October, 2012, on the Prosecution's third 92 bis motion. The Prosecution submits that the Chamber erred in denying admission of portions of the witness's testimony because the evidence at issue is relevant and necessary for a full understanding of the testimony provisionally admitted by the Chamber. The Prosecution further submits that the evidence is reasonably related to the witness's Rule 65 ter summary, citing the Chamber's previous guidance on the matter in relation to Rule 92 bis witnesses. For these reason, the Prosecution requests reconsideration of the decision and the admission of an additional 30 transcript pages of the witness's previous testimony. The Chamber is satisfied that the Prosecution's additional submissions on relevance and probative value amount to particular circumstances justifying reconsideration in order to avoid injustice. Having reviewed the tendered evidence again in light of these more detailed submissions, the Chamber agrees that the tendered evidence provides valuable context and a clearer understanding of the evidence which was provisionally admitted by the Chamber's 4th of October decision. The Chamber finds, therefore, that the tendered transcript pages are sufficiently relevant to and probative of Counts 2 through 8 of the indictment for admission into evidence. For the foregoing reasons, the Chamber hereby grants the Prosecution's motion and: 1, admits the additional transcript pages from Ljubomir Mitrovic's previous testimony as listed in Annex A of the motion, and confirms the admission of the transcript pages of Mitrovic's previous testimony that were provisionally admitted in the 4th of October decision; 2, instructs the Prosecution to upload within two weeks of this decision the newly admitted transcript excerpts along with those previously admitted by the Chamber so that all of the witness's admitted testimony is available under one Rule 65 ter number; and, 3, instructs the Registry to assign an exhibit number to the admitted evidence and inform the parties and the Chamber of the number so assigned. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just I'd request to be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the usher is invited to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to go onto another topic which you touched upon, the military judicial organs and their functioning. First of all, having studied the normative structures of the VRS and Republika Srpska, can you confirm whether or not the military courts and military prosecutors were subordinated to the Main Staff of the VRS or not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that Your Honours because the documents I have reviewed do not indicate -- do not indicate such a subordination. I can only state that they were established pursuant to an order of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did your review reveal that the military courts were under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I'm just going through the -- through my report. You have to be aware there is an order - this is on page 100, and maybe I have to correct my previous answer. Page 100 of Part 2 of the report, there is an order by the RS president, i.e., Mr. Karadzic, to place the military courts, the supreme military court, and the prosecutor's office attached to the Main Staff of the VRS under his direct authority; i.e., under the authority of Mr. Karadzic. I believe that this is the only document I have reviewed that provides information as to whom these organs are subordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your -- did your review of the materials indicate whether General Mladic had any power to appoint or promote prosecutors and judges of the military courts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not seen any documents indicating that General Karadzic appointed prosecutors or judges in the military courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, earlier you made Mr. Arkan a general. You're now making Mr. Karadzic a general --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Mladic appointing prosecutors or judges. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague Judge Fluegge says what about promotions? Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The next topic I would like to raise with you relates to the Supreme Command which is an organ you discuss in Part 1 page 20 and Part 2 pages 61 through 63 of your report. For the record, can you confirm for us that neither General Mladic, nor his deputy commander, nor any of his assistant commanders from the Main Staff were members of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And I have explained that also on page 62 of Part 2. They can, however, attend on invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In relation to the authority to assign army forces to positions within the VRS and to promote or demote the same from command establishment posts, was this a power held in the hands of General Mladic and the Main Staff or was it a power held by the Supreme Command or the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends of the -- of the level, Your Honours, and there was also a change in the course of the conflict. But at least initially -- or, I mean, upon a certain time, General Mladic had the authority to appoint and demote and to promote officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to Part 3 of your report, pages 352 to the end, you detail the tensions between the VRS and General Mladic on the one hand, and the RS president on the other. At page 353, you indicate relations deteriorated in the course of 1994 and that by spring 1995 things get worse such that by April 1995 you describe it as an open conflict. Is it correct that especially during this time-period, the RS president and Supreme Command attempted to bypass General Mladic and issue orders directly to VRS units?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, the conclusion is -- the suggestion is too strong. I have, if I remember well, cited one example where General Mladic intervenes. This has to do with the SRK, then under the command of General Dragomir Milosevic where General Mladic suspects that General Milosevic is about to use, I believe, modified air-bombs in the Sarajevo area without the authorisation, i.e., the order of the General Mladic, and then General Mladic intervenes in order to rectify the situation. So this is an example of where he suspects that General Milosevic gets his orders from somewhere else instead of from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that your discussion about the situational awareness of General Mladic and the effectiveness of his command and control over the VRS on paper would have to take into account such circumstances of the political leadership and Supreme Command sending orders directly to VRS units?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know what the reference to command and control over the VRS on paper means. I mean, I have not seen a document by General Mladic indicating that he cannot exercise command and control over the VRS, and I mean during the May 1992 to November 1995 time-period. Answering the question then. Well, I mean, I have included a section on the discussion -- to discuss these tensions and even on what I call an open conflict, I mean, based on the two and a half hour speech General Mladic gives at an assembly session in spring 1995, and then also the attempts by President Karadzic to change the job title of General Mladic in -- in August 1995, and how then all the corps commanders express their loyalty to General Mladic, and at the end of the story, Mr. Karadzic is forced to withdraw his order on redefining the -- the position or the job description of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to move to another topic. In your report you have talked of restrictions upon UNPROFOR and actions of the VRS as to UNPROFOR. This is generally in Part 3, contained in pages 295 to 318, and relates also to the so-called hostage crisis in May through June 1995. Based upon your review of documentation, and based upon your own experiences in the field, did you see evidence that UNPROFOR was increasingly siding against the Bosnian Serbs and thus engaging in mission creep to become more in the a way of a combatant party on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just keeping track of the record, there has been two references to Part 3 of the report. However, there are only two parts to the report. I believe that's part 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Part 2. Part 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not see such evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to look at 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- the question was based on your review of documentation and based upon your own experience in the field, so if you said I didn't see such evidence, that -- your own experience is usually not visible. Have you considered that part of the question as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my answer covered both parts of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's -- my question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up 1D1495 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for the same, I can introduce it as a declassified US State Department telex dated 28 May 1995. And, sir, I would like to direct your attention to paragraphs 2 and 3 on the first page, and once we finish with those, the short conclusion in paragraph 5 which read as follows: "2. We had a short meeting with General Smith on May 28. There was nothing new. He reiterated that the machine is essentially broken, and the bleak alternative is to 'make war' or to become unsustainably weak. To refine the mandate and configuration of UNPROFOR is to avoid the essential '1.000 dollar question.' In fact, a reconfiguration or redeployment simply 'pretends that we are making war' when we are not. "3. Redefinition of the mandate is to continue the 'non-war mode.' There is no really middle ground between war and the abandonment of the UNPROFOR mission. The stark decision remains 'we either fight or we don't.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "5. Comment: Smith has been making his case to the UN and others that UNPROFOR is essentially finished. To attempt to walk some middle ground between war and withdrawal is a delusion. End comment." Is such information about the activities of General Smith in campaigning for a move of the UNPROFOR mission to be one of making war, something that you had information on when performing your research for the expert report that you drafted in this case.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that Mr. Ivetic's proposition is -- is simplistic. You to have look at the context in which General Smith, at least according to this transcript, made certain comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you for a second. Mr. Ivetic in his question qualified what Mr. Smith did. Let's leave out that qualification and let's focus on what is described in the document. And then, now, the question is whether you considered the activities of General Smith when preparing your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't have any information concerning this meeting General Smith, who was the commander -- Force Commander of UNPROFOR in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time when I was preparing my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware of information which deals with the position of General Smith in relation to strength, weakness, continuation, or discontinuation of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I know Your Honours, and at that time I was working as a military information officer in the UNPA headquarters in Zagreb, was that there was a high degree of division within the international community as to what UNPROFOR should do because international community, I mean, was divided and was also losing its patience with the parties in the conflict, and on the ground there were, I would almost call it, surreal scenes where the parties - I mean, the ABiH and the VRS - were fighting each other at times in Sarajevo with UN vehicles. So that -- I mean, there was serious concern about whether the mandate, as it had been defined, was -- could still be implemented, what the support of the international community was for that mandate, and then how the force, UNPROFOR, was to implement that mandate. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you consider that when writing your report or is this because you specifically refer to your previous position and your awareness of these problems not on documentation? Is it underlying your report this information as well or is it just that you now being asked about it tell us about it, where it played no role in the drafting of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it -- I didn't refer to this in my report because indeed, as you pointed out, it is not of direct relevance for my report. But, of course, when I discussed hostage crisis, I refer to certain activities that had taken place just prior to the hostage crisis, but I didn't go into specificities as I have discussed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I expressed myself on the direct relevance of it, but apart from that thank you for your answer. Mr. Ivetic may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence would tender the document into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the Prosecution please have more information on the provenance? We do not find a ERN number that's associated --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- with anything in our system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The source of the document is the CIA. It's available from the CIA's web site of 300 documents recently disclosed. The date of the disclosure is at the top of the page, March 19th, 2013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the CIA web side?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very well. Well, I mean, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1495 receives number D452, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D452 is admitted into evidence, and the Prosecution has an opportunity to revisit the origin of this document if it wishes to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I can provide the -- the link as soon as I finish with my cross, that would perhaps assist the Prosecution in determining if they have any further submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may revisit the matter if -- but then let's do it this week and not any later. Or report to the Chamber if you need more time. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to turn to another topic. During your direct examination, specifically at transcript page 20240 through 20241, you testified about General Mladic being out in the field actively leading combat operations and that there are several examples of that as included in your report. I'd like to ask you in this regard if your reference to your report was in relation to Part 2 pages 344 to 352 where you talk about visits and inspections and meetings in the field, or if there are some other part of your report that you claim gives evidence of General Mladic leading combat operations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this context it is also relevant to look at page 245 of Part 2, i.e., footnote 925, because there's a whole series of documents there that refer to forward command posts, including some that were -- where General Mladic was -- was present. And I believe also in the section, when I'm talking about the operations in eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina about situation in and around Srebrenica in July 1995, as well as - I'm sorry for the disorder, but also March/April 1994 in the wider area of Gorazde, that there are several documents from the VRS Main Staff as well as from the -- the -- the Drina Corps. And even -- for Srebrenica, I think from -- there are notes of the -- the MUP commander in the area all highlighting the -- the role of General Mladic in the operations that the VRS is conducting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to present you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, let me -- I'm trying to look at 20240.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It starts at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- line 15 through line 2 on 20241.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you've seen it. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to present you with something which General Dannatt testified about in our case which is to be found at transcript page 19175, line 8, through 19176, line 4, which went as follows: "Q. Now I'd like to move on to General Mladic's presence on the ground in Srebrenica and the Hotel Fontana that you testified about yesterday. At transcript page 19071 you talked of Mladic keeping close control and issuing directions. I wish to now take a look at part of your testimony from the Krstic case. "Mr. Ivetic: 1D1444, page 71 of the same, which should correlate to transcript page 5713 of underlying document. If we could focus on lines 24 to 25 for the question and then we will have to turn the page for the answer, which is on lines 1 through 4. "Q. Sir, I read: 'Judge Riad: But there was no sign of General Mladic giving direct orders to the subordinates of General Krstic? "'A. No, sir. I don't think we've -- I think we've looked at that several times previously, and I can see no evidence of General Mladic giving orders to constituent parts of the Drina Corps and therefore bypassing the normal corps command and control structure. I don't see any evidence of that.' "Do you stand by this testimony as being truthful such that you would so repeat the same today? "A. Absolutely. I don't see any evidence of that. That's not to say it didn't happen. But I don't see and didn't see any evidence of that." Do you agree or disagree with General Sir Richard Dannatt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's make that question quite clear. Is the question whether Mr. Theunens agrees that Mr. Dannatt did not see evidence or that it did not happen? Because MR. Dannatt says it may well have happened but I've not seen the evidence. Now, what precisely is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The question is -- well, let me rephrase the question then to make it absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there is no evidence of General Mladic giving direct orders to constituent parts of the Drina Corps and therefore bypassing the normal corps command and control structure?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not seen a Drina Corps document or a VRS document that would make that suggestion. However, as I mentioned earlier, there is the report by Ljubisav Borovcanin, who was commander of a special police brigade, and this is footnote 1046 of Part 2 of report who -- who writes in his report that that General Mladic is personally in command of the combat operations in the wider Srebrenica area. Again, this is, when I refer back to my methodology, one observation made by one senior official who was in the Srebrenica area. We would will have to look at more material, which I haven't done, in order to draw a conclusion that would allow to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. You've mentioned the police. I'd like to now go to my last topic which is in relation to the MUP or the police forces. I believe you have discussed this at, among other places, Part 2 pages 35 through 36 and 71 through 72, and you also testified about it during your direct examination at transcript page 20382 in relation to police and VRS activities at Trnovo. I'd like to first ask you: In respect of your review and analysis of JNA and SFRY doctrinal documents, did you have occasion to come across the concept of "co-ordinated action" or as it is called in the B/C/S "sadejstvo" as a recognised method of two units from different formations or organisations operating within the same battle-field or operation such as when MUP or police units operate alongside the army?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible to break this question up? I don't understand the question, Mr. Ivetic. It's so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me start at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. No. Let's -- it -- it -- even -- let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can ask if he's familiar with the concept of "sadejstvo" or co-ordinated action. I think that's -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you take it step by step, that would be good.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did your research reveal a concept of co-ordinated action or "sadejstvo" in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did, Your Honours, and you can find that in Part 1 of the report, English page 34 and 35, as one of the functions of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And is co-ordinated action or "sadejstvo" a method by which two units from different organisations can operate within the same battle-field or operation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you also agree that "sadejstvo" or co-ordinated action is a different method of operation than resubordination?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I'm not sure I understand what you are -- what the question is, and maybe I can clarify it by referring to an extract from the corps of ground forces regulation that I put on English page 35, part 1, where I say that the commander is the one who organises the implementation of co-ordination among all participants for the execution of a combat assignment, whereas the Chief of Staff of the corps, I mean, this is when the -- the corps was in command co-ordinates the work of the commands. So this means when unit A and unit B have to co-ordinate their operations, there is no subordination relation between unit A and unit B. However, above these two units there is, of course, a commander who orders and instructs how these two units are to co-ordinate their operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that an analysis of a particular operation must take into account both reviewing to see whether it was co-ordinated action or resubordination that was at play?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the specific documents, i.e., the orders -- I mean, you have seen all those, the combat documents and the reporting -- I mean, the orders and the reporting documents will show what kind of relation exists between the units that are conducting the operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to go -- talk about resubordination of the police to army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could I ask one question in relation to one of the previous questions. You were asked about General Mladic being in the field commanding operations. You referred to some documents in relation to Srebrenica and Gorazde, I think. Did you consider only documentary evidence in that respect, because the Chamber has seen a video in which General Mladic is walking through the streets - that's at least how it was explained - and giving orders, instructions. Did you consider that as well, or are you familiar with that video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if -- if you refer to a video on -- on situation in Srebrenica, I am indeed familiar with the video. I didn't use videos because I consider that the primary documents I had were of sufficient, I mean, clarity and value to -- to draw conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the Chamber has seen this video, and just on the basis of the assumption that you've seen the same video, would that -- could the Chamber understand such a video as corroboration of what is found in the documentary evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In -- in my view, yes, Your Honours. I mean, you would have to look at the two and see that they discuss the same events and the same time-frame, and then indeed one would illustrate the other or would corroborate the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I just was wondering whether or not you had included that in your conclusions or not and, of course, how the Chamber has to -- to deal with that in an appropriate way. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you consider yourself knowledgeable as an expert on the topic of the resubordination of the police to the army?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will not go again in the point of expert because I have mentioned that already a few times. But I have looked at all these, I mean, the various VRS and also MUP documents, to see how the units operated, and again they are very straightforward. So I drew certain conclusions on the basis of the documents I reviewed, irrespective of whether those consisted of documents discussing the MUP or the military. There are indeed documents that, I mean, for example, Trnovo, but I don't believe I have discussed that here in detail, but I remember from my report for the Stanisic Simatovic case that indeed MUP units are operating in the wider Trnovo area in, I believe, May and the subsequent -- I mean, May, June, or even July 1995, there and are also some orders in relation to that by General Mladic; for example, on the use of the a helicopter to evacuate injured MUP and I believe it's RSK, MUP RSK members.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based upon your review of the material and knowledge of the same, would you agree that police units resubordinated to the army for purposes of combat retain their police commanders during said combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, isn't there an internal contradiction in your question? Police units resubordinated retained their -- the command of their -- their commanders? You've just said they are resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They are. And that is what is according to the amended Law of the Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska, sir, that their individual unit police commanders remained the same in the -- in the conduct of the combat. And I'm asking the individual if can he confirm that based upon his review of the documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see whether I understand the question. Resubordination - but please correct me when I'm wrong - means that a unit is made part of a military structure and put under the command of the higher unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A subordinated or resubordinated unit is still acting under the command of its own commander, although where the unit is subordinated or resubordinated, that commander is also under the command of the higher-up level. Is that a proper understanding of command positions in a subordinated or resubordinated situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't want to add to the confusion, but looking at SFRY armed forces terminology, the resubordination is only used for establishment units; i.e., for example, if a tank company of a tank battalion that is part of brigade A is resubordinated to an infantry battalion of brigade A. So they have the same establishment unit. In the other case, for example, if a TO unit would be subordinated to a JNA unit, we talk about reattachment. The same would be the situation with a MUP unit that is subordinated to a military unit. In JNA parlance we would use -- we would say that the MUP unit was reattached to the JNA unit. Answering your question, well, the principle of single command and control means that it can only be one commander at a time. So maybe with an example. If, say, a police company, police company A, is to conduct combat operations as being attached to a VRS battalion, call it B, in a specific area: Based on the documents I have seen, all the orders concerning those specific operations come from that VRS battalion commander. Of course, the commander -- I mean, the unit commander, the company commander of the police company who is in the field with his police company, he can he still send reports to his organic MUP battalion or -- or Ministry of Interior authority or commander, but the latter should have no influence on the actual operations that are being conducted by the MUP unit, the MUP company, that has been reattached or as we call it here resubordinated to the VRS infantry battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the MUP commander under those circumstances would receive his orders, operational orders exclusively from the VRS command which is above him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, for the time-period that they are to conduct operations. And you expect that in such a situation there is -- I mean, co-ordination or contact between the higher echelon of the battalion and the higher echelon of the MUP unit because they have to -- it's not the battalion that will order the MUP unit to come to that area, like to Trnovo, at a specific date. That has been decided at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can just clarify, sir, your discussion started off being very precise, and then in answer to the questions of Judge Orie, you averted to saying operations. By "operations" do you specifically mean combat operations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. Or it could also be for an exercise or for training. That -- yes. And again, the combat documents, be it the reporting documents or the command documents, will show very clearly who is in command of what. And for during which time-period. But I gave you the general principles that should be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I am looking at the clock. I'm doing it only four times a day, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I have four questions precisely to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then perhaps we -- we allow you to proceed with those four questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that after combat is completed and that the police units returned to their police work, they are no longer resubordinated to the army officers?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, from a generic point of view I would agree, but, you know, we have to look at the specific documents because they will state who is in charge when.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree that after police forces complete their combat and are no longer at the front lines, they are off duty and no longer performing tasks pursuant to military orders under resubordination?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it depends of the specific documents. I mean, what is -- when -- [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about police forces that frolic and detour from their official assignments to engage in personal crimes of opportunity, would you agree that they would fall under the disciplinary remit of the civilian police organs?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I would ask for further clarification. Where are these units? Are they just -- I mean, are they in Belgrade or are they in -- on an area where there are military conducting combat operations? I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So would you agree with me, it depends a lot on the specific facts and circumstances that must be examined carefully?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason why I made the comment is that if they're doing these things while they are conducting operations under the command of a military unit, and again given the 1988 regulations on implementation of the laws of war by the JNA, which were also applied by the VRS, the VRS commander in the area where the MUP units were has the duty to investigate these alleged crimes. As to the enforcement of -- I mean, further enforcement of discipline and justice, this -- this resides then with -- with the -- the police hierarchy. Unless there is a different arrangement between the superior MUP echelon and the superior military echelon, but I haven't seen any documents on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one point of clarification. I take the situation where a police company is attached to or subordinated to the VRS. When that takes an end, and if that police company moves out but still is in the zone of responsibility of the previous VRS command over it, if they would commit crimes then, what would be the situation? Because you referred to the duty to investigate. Is -- would that still be the duty for the commander? It's more or less a legal question, as a matter of fact, but if you have any opinion about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, from the military point of view, there is no such situation that units are just wondering around. There is one commander and he is responsible for the situation in his zone of operations. And if formally, I mean, based on the documents, the attachment of subordination of that police unit would have finished, then they have to -- they have to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At a certain moment, well, let's say at 12.00 at night, the resubordination ends, which means that the police unit would then be under its normal command structures again, which would then tell them come home or go there or go to A, go to B. Now as long as they are still in the zone of responsibility of the previous VRS commander over them, in following their orders to go to A or B but still being in the zone of responsibility of the VRS, which commander would have a duty to investigate, in your view, if the crime is committed after 12.00 but the unit still being in the zone of responsibility of the previous VRS command which existed until 12.00? If you don't have an answer to the question, then please tell us. But you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't investigate or analyse the MUP here, but again I with give you the military flavour of or the military aspect of the situation, that is: A commander is responsible for what's happening in his zone of responsibility, even if there are units there that are not under his subordination anymore. He has to be familiar with the situation also. So even probably legally it is not his duty to investigate what this police unit that is not under his subordination anymore has allegedly been doing, I mean, military common sense would dictate that he will try to gather information because he will hearing something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And he will then share that information with the superiors of the MUP and he will do that in writing. And then it's up to the MUP to take the -- the -- the subsequent measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think you were at the third of your four questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked for the fourth so I'm done. I thank you for the indulgence of the extra several minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an application that may be important to raise now. Your Honours, I'm going to ask that we adjourn with the evidence of Mr. Theunens today and continue with the re-direct examination on Thursday. I think the cross-examination transpired in a way that I do not think was envisaged by the Chamber when it gave its guidance. The guidance has also attached significant consequences to how the Prosecution conducts its re-direct. The Prosecution would like to consider its position and its re-direct in light of this and other things that occurred during the examination. I would ask that the re-direct examination commence on Thursday, and I am very confident that the re-direct examination will conclude well before the end of the court day on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And still sufficient time then for the Defence to ask further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm confident in that as well, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is included in your estimate --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you would conclude. Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We take no position. It's up to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber accepts your suggestion, Mr. Groome, but would then deal with a few procedural matters for the last half-hour of today. So we'll advance some of the procedural matters, not all of them but there are a few still to be dealt with so that we don't spend time on that on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Theunens, you followed the discussion. Although we have not finished for the day, nevertheless you have, at least in this courtroom. I again instruct you, for the last time, I take it, that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, and we'd like to see you back Thursday morning at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, III.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Theunens be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we'll resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I announced, we'll spend some time on dealing with procedural matters. The first deals with a change of status of exhibits from the first intercept bar table motion and replacement of P1231. On the 8th of November, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to provide the Chamber with any additional updates in relation to the confidential status of exhibits admitted pursuant to the Chamber's 2nd of May, 2013, decision on the first intercept bar table motion. On the 12th of November, the Prosecution filed its request to lift the confidential status of several intercepts. The Prosecution also proposed to correct an error in the redaction of Exhibit P1231 and submitted that the remaining intercepts should retain their confidential status to protect the identity of the intercept operators and/or the locations of the relevant communications facilities. The Defence did not file a response. Having considered the Prosecution's submissions in relation to the content of the intercepts, the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to change the status of the exhibits as identified by the Prosecution in paragraphs 1 and 2 of its notice from confidential to public, and to retain the confidential status of the remaining intercepts admitted in the Chamber's decision of the 2nd of May. Lastly, the Chamber instructs the Registry to replace the B/C/S original of P1231 with document ID number 0080-4826-RED. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on this matter. We now briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber had turned into private session to deliver its decision admitting Exhibit P2365. I will now address a number of remaining evidentiary issues related to exhibits used by the parties during Witness Butler's testimony. First, concerning P2099, the Chamber considered the Defence objection set out in their informal communication of the 18th of November, as well as the Prosecution's response set out in their informal communication of the same date, both of which are now hereby put on the record. The Prosecution stated that it is prepared to address the authenticity of this document further and provide further information in its support. The Chamber would invite the Prosecution to do so within seven days through a filing. Second, the Chamber admits into evidence the relevant extracts of the Official Gazette uploaded by the Prosecution under Rule 65 ter number 04387a as Exhibit P2104. Should the Defence wish to rely on other parts, other extracts of these laws, it can proceed to tender them. Third, as to P2105, the Chamber has taken notice of the parties' agreement as to the date featured in that document, filed on the 18th of November, and admits P2105 into evidence. There is no need to have the document containing the parties' agreement in this respect admitted into evidence or added to the Prosecution's 65 ter exhibit list; thus, the Prosecution motion of the 3rd of December to that effect is denied. Fourth, the Chamber took note of the Prosecution submission that P2126 concerns the same communication as P1322 and admitted P2126 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. You are hiding behind a pillar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry for reappearing like this. On your ruling that you just made, I just wanted to discuss that briefly with Mr. Groome, the -- the stipulation regarding the -- I believe it was the date of an intercept, I think we agreed that -- that the 13th was what was on the document, something that we -- and if we don't file that as part of the evidence, how will you know to be able to -- if that becomes relevant in a judgement, how will you know on when -- what date to conclude that if we don't have it in evidence? I just -- that's the reason why we filed it, so that you would have access to that date for any judgement or any other use you wanted to make of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We keep track of every decision we take, including taking notice of the agreement among parties. But you'd say that it may not be -- we only say here that it was the document filed on the 18th of November which does not give yet the information relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I think what we filed was the stipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The reason we did that was because we felt that for you to use -- use that date, the 13th of July intercept date in a judgement, you would need to have it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I tend to agree with you that I have not put the agreement on the record yet. We will consider whether we will do that orally later or whether we would still -- we would still have the document -- we'll reconsider whether we rightly or wrongly denied the motion of the 3rd of December in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on that topic, I know something that you have encouraged us to do and we have done, is we informally agree on thing on the record, and we -- we're not quite sure among the parties where that fits in the record. Is it something you will be able to refer to in a -- in a judgement, be whatever issue you're -- you're dealing with. Normally the most conservative way is that it -- such agreements get entered into the evidence, but I wasn't sure what the Court had in mind and I -- I -- and really do like being able to informally agree on the record, it saves a lot of time, but I'm not sure - and I know Mr. Groome and I have discussed this - we were not precisely sure where -- what the legal status of these agreements were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the content of the agreement is clear and if it has been read out or referred to in the necessary detail on the transcript, then the transcript is part of the record of this case and we can rely on whatever is found on the transcript as an agreement between the parties. But then, of course, I do agree with you that the content of the agreement should be clear as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a further look at P2105 to see whether that needs further explanation. We'll just have a look at it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the Defence any specific position in relation to how to put this agreement on the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I come from a jurisdiction where filings are part of the court record and are official. That's the way we've dealt with at least two other stipulations that I've been a party -- a part of in this case. I'm at Your Honours' suggestion. Any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we've made the stipulation. We don't back off from it. So whichever way works for everyone, as long as we just know what that is, that should be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any chance that you come from the same jurisdiction and not -- or at least close?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Close, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We do recognise Illinois in California, but not much. The -- the written stipulation was a classic agreement where it's subtle enough that it's better from the writing than it would be something that we orally would go to. So we both agree that the writing is what to focus on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I continue. I had dealt with the fourth item. I now move to the fifth one. The Chamber took note of the Prosecution's intention to rely, in addition to Chapter 16 of the SFRY Criminal Code, on chapters 3, 15, and 20, and instructs the Registry to replace Exhibit P2183 with document bearing Rule 65 ter number 04379b. Turning to P2189 and P1153, the Chamber takes note of the parties agreement on the wording of the revised translations and instructs the Registry to replace the English versions currently in e-court with documents with ID numbers 0087-6290-ET and 0430-2969-1-ET respectively. It also admits P2189 into evidence. As to P2137, the Chamber instructs the Registry to replace the version currently in e-court with the document as reorganised by the Prosecution following the Chamber's instructions of the 9th of September and bearing Rule 65 ter number 05130a. Turning to D285, the Chamber takes note of the parties' agreement that the document with Rule 65 ter number 04205c should replace the document currently uploaded as Exhibit D285 and instructs the Registry to replace it accordingly. As to P2192, the Chamber took note of the Prosecution submissions made in its formal communication of the 20th of November, which is now put on the record, that this intercept was part of 34 binders of intercepts obtained by the Prosecution from the 2nd Corps in Tuzla on the 26th of December, 2000, which were photocopied in The Hague and were then returned to the 2nd Corps. In light of these submission, the Chamber rejects the Defence objection of the 16th of September and admits P2192 into evidence. The Chamber takes note of the Defence submission set out in its informal communication of the 20th of November, which is hereby put on the record, that it has not been in a position to obtain the original of the document uploaded in e-court as D360. Considering the present stage of the proceedings, admission of D360 is denied without prejudice. As to P2198, the Chamber has taken note of the Defence position that the French original refers to the hostage crisis using quotation marks. With regard to P1968, the Chamber took note of the outcome of the Prosecution's enquiries with CLSS regarding the sentence in Directive 4 on page 5 of the English version and page 11 of the B/C/S under item (d) in that CLSS has confirmed that the words "able-bodied and armed men" and -- in the English translation reflect the B/C/S original. Lastly, the Chamber took note of the parties' agreement that the word "glavni" on page 79 of the English version and page 78 of the B/C/S version of P1501, the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook, can be translated to "boss" as well as to "the main one." And this concludes the Chamber's instructions on these matters. Turning to the Prosecution's motion for admission of excerpts of Witness Butler's original Srebrenica military narrative expert report, filed on the 3rd of December, 2013, the Chamber recalls that on the 14th of November, it admitted all of Witness Butler's expert reports with the exception of the original Srebrenica narrative given the extent of the latter's overlap with the revised Srebrenica narrative. The Prosecution now seeks to admit two chapters of the original narrative together with its list of references which, in their submission, are relevant and probative. Given that the matter seems to be relatively straightforward, the Chamber would like to inquire whether the Defence is prepared to state its position on admission of these two chapters and the list of references.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Then Prosecution, could the Prosecution tell us which 65 ter number includes the two chapter and the lists of references so that a number can be assigned and that we can decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, perhaps I have misunderstood you. Yes, you said you could state your position and I have not invited you, which I should have done, to then give that position. Perhaps I was optimistic about -- but please, have you an opportunity to state your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We had objected to the -- both Srebrenica narratives being introduced. Your Honours had admitted one over that objection and then this motion was filed. We make no further submissions as to the motion filed the 6th of December for the two excerpts. We would restate our position as being the same as before, that we object to the narratives being introduced as expert testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But have you no specific problems with having only two chapters now thus avoiding the overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But your objection stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection - may not come as a great surprise, Mr. Ivetic - is overruled. The Prosecution is invited to communicate what 65 ter number will be used for this -- these excerpts and the references. And if you don't know yet, we'll just invite Madam Registrar to already reserve a number for it. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The reserved number would be P3077, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'd like to hear the 65 ter number as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The 65 ter number will be 446269. Oh, I'm sorry. 46 -- 4626A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is uploaded already or will it be -- it will be uploaded under this number. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: By the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the end of the day. And this is the document which is then -- which is P3077. It is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, if you want to revisit it, not having seen at this moment, the uploaded document, you can do so, but not later than this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, just a clarification: On page 86, line 19, the line should read: "It also admits P2189 into evidence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the advantage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should read "it also admits P2189." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the advantage of having three Judges on the Bench which all have experience as Presiding Judges. I am a bit in doubt. I have one more decision, which is two pages, to be read. We could do it now so that we have dealt with all the procedural issues, as far as I'm concerned. I would prefer that, but I would not force any of those assisting us into such a situation. Neither would I force Mr. Mladic in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would then finally deliver a short decision. It's a decision on the admission of P2515 and P2516. On September the 13th, the Prosecution filed a Rule 92 ter motion relating to witness Jeremy Bowen in which it tendered, inter alia, Bowen's 10th of August, 2009, witness statements and excerpts of his prior testimony from the Prosecutor versus Karadzic case dated 13th and 14th of January, 2011. On the 27th of September, the Defence responded to the Prosecution's motion, objecting to the statement and the excerpts of prior testimony on the basis that: 1, portions contain significant evidence going directly to the accused's acts and conduct as well as his personal knowledge; 2, portions include opinion-type testimony which is improper expert or quasi-expert in nature which has not been submitted via Rule 94 bis; 3, they include unreliable hearsay; 4, the excerpts of prior testimony do not include prior cross-examination; and, 5, the statement includes matters outside the scope of the indictment. On the 17th of October, 2013, the Prosecution tendered -- Mr. Mladic, I would not mind if you do not interrupt me. On the 17th of October, 2013, the Prosecution tendered the statement and the excerpts of the prior testimony through Bowen in court. The Defence confirmed that it had no further objections apart from what can be found in its 27th of September response. The documents were marked for identification as P2515 and P2516 respectively. On the 21st of October, the Prosecution indicated in court that it would contact the Defence to see if an agreement could be reached on P2515 and P2516. On the 14th of November, 2013, the Prosecution reported to the Chamber, in court, that no agreement had been reached as to the Defence's objections that P2515 and P2516 contain expert or opinion testimony and unreliable hearsay testimony. With regard to the Defence's objection concerning opinion-type testimony, which is improper expert or quasi-expert in nature, the Chamber refers to its 6th of September, 2012, guidance on this matter. Further, the Chamber considers that the portions of P2515 and P2516 which the Defence cites in this context do not constitute expert testimony but are, rather, the witness's accounts of events he had learned of. With regard to the Defence's objection concerning hearsay evidence, the Chamber again refers to its 6th of September, 2012, guidance on this matter and recalls that hearsay evidence is, in principle, admissible in proceedings before the Tribunal, and that the weight to be attributed to it by the Chamber will be assessed in light of all the evidence before it. With regard to the portions of evidence identified by the Defence in this respect, the Chamber finds that either the source of knowledge is stated in the evidence, or that it is clear that the witness has no direct knowledge of certain matters he testified about. While the Chamber notes that P2515 and P2516 contain some hearsay evidence, it considers that these portions do not affect the evidence's overall probative value. For the foregoing reasons, the Chamber denies the Defence's request to strike the portions identified from the documents, and admits [Realtime transcript read in error "admitted"] P2515 and P2516 into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision.
